title.zh: 卷八十上 文苑列傳
title.raw: 卷八十上 文苑列傳 Volume 80a: Biographies of Writers 1

sentences.zh: 杜笃字季雅，京兆杜陵人也。

translations.literal: Du Du, courtesy name Jiya, was a man of Duling in the capital region of Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du, whose courtesy name was Jiya, came from Duling in the metropolitan area around the capital.

sentences.zh: 高祖延年，宣帝时为御史大夫。

translations.literal: His ancestor of the high founding line was Yannian, who under Emperor Xuan served as imperial secretary.
translations.idiomatic: His forebear Yannian of the founding line had been imperial secretary under Emperor Xuan.

sentences.zh: 笃少博学，不修小节，不为乡人所礼。

translations.literal: In youth Du was broadly learned, did not cultivate minor points of conduct, and was not treated with respect by his fellow villagers.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man he read widely but scorned petty etiquette, and the people of his village did not hold him in esteem.

sentences.zh: 居美阳，与美阳令游，数从请托，不谐，颇相恨。

translations.literal: He resided in Meiyang and associated with the magistrate of Meiyang; repeatedly he made requests and entreatments through him; they did not go well, and they came to resent each other considerably.
translations.idiomatic: He lived at Meiyang and kept company with its magistrate, often asking favors through him; when those overtures failed, the two grew mutually bitter.

translations.literal: The magistrate, enraged, seized Du and sent him to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate, in a fury, had him arrested and escorted to the capital.

sentences.zh: 会大司马吴汉薨，光武诏诸儒诔之，笃于狱中为诔，辞最高，美帝之，赐帛免刑。

translations.literal: It happened that Grand Marshal Wu Han died; Guangwu ordered the scholars to compose dirges for him. Du, in prison, wrote a dirge; his wording ranked highest; the emperor praised it and granted him silk, remitting his punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Just then Grand Marshal Wu Han died, and Guangwu summoned the literati to compose laments. From his cell Du Du produced one judged the finest; the emperor admired it, awarded him silk, and spared him further punishment.

sentences.zh: 笃以关中表里山河，先帝旧京，不宜改营洛邑，乃上奏《论都赋》曰：

translations.literal: Du held that within the passes mountains and rivers formed inner and outer ramparts, that it was the former capital of the prior emperors, and that it was inappropriate to shift the seat and build at Luoyang; therefore he presented a memorial titled "Rhapsody on the Capital," saying:
translations.idiomatic: Du Du argued that the Guanzhong heartland was shielded by mountains and rivers, that it had been the old capital of the Han founders, and that abandoning it for Luoyang was unwise; he therefore submitted his "Rhapsody on the Capital" in memorial form, which begins:

sentences.zh: 臣闻知而复知，是为重知。

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that to know and again to know is called double knowing.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard it said: to be told what one already knows is merely redundant knowledge.

sentences.zh: 臣所欲言，陛下已知，故略其梗概，不敢具陈。

translations.literal: What your subject wishes to speak, Your Majesty already knows; therefore I abbreviate the outline and dare not set it forth in full.
translations.idiomatic: What I would say you already understand; I shall only sketch its gist and not rehearse every detail.

translations.literal: In antiquity Pan Geng cast off extravagance and practiced frugality at Bo.
translations.idiomatic: Long ago Pan Geng renounced luxury and practiced austerity when he dwelt at Bo.

translations.literal: At the height of Chengzhou, then they settled in central Luo.
translations.idiomatic: When Chengzhou flourished, the royal house fixed itself in the central Luo plain.

translations.literal: Meeting the times they regulated the capital; they did not permanently fix their city.
translations.idiomatic: Each age set its capital as circumstance demanded; no single site was held forever.

translations.literal: The deliberations of the worthy and sage, in general, had strengths and weaknesses.
translations.idiomatic: Even sages weighed such choices differently, some plans proving stronger than others.

translations.literal: The bearing of hegemons and kings, clear knowledge was mutually far apart.
translations.idiomatic: The posture of a hegemon and that of a true king spring from insight worlds apart.

translations.literal: The posture of guarding the state: the same goal, different methods.
translations.idiomatic: Defending a realm may aim at the same end yet follow contrary strategies.

translations.literal: Some cast away barrier passes and peril and strove to dwell on level, easy ground.
translations.idiomatic: Some forsook defiles and rugged terrain for open, tractable country.

translations.literal: Some relied on mountains and girded with rivers, swallowing the six states.
translations.idiomatic: Some hugged mountains and rivers and so swallowed the six rival kingdoms.

translations.literal: Some, when rich and noble, thought of returning home and did not care about being attacked from behind.
translations.idiomatic: Some, grown wealthy and exalted, longed for home and ignored the risk of a stab in the back.

sentences.zh: 或掩空击虚，自蜀汉出，即日车驾，策由一卒；

translations.literal: Some struck empty space and hit the void, coming out from Ba and Shu; that very day the imperial carriages; the plan came from one soldier.
translations.idiomatic: Some struck where defenses were thin, marching straight from Ba and Shu so that the imperial train rolled out in a day on a plan hatched by a single soldier.

translations.literal: Some knew but did not follow, long dwelling on barren heights.
translations.idiomatic: Some knew better yet refused to move, clinging for ages to bleak high ground.

translations.literal: Your subject does not dare to rely on anything fixed.
translations.idiomatic: I do not presume to insist on any one doctrine.

sentences.zh: 窃见司马相如、杨子云作辞赋以讽主上，臣诚慕之，伏作书一篇，名曰《论都》，谨并封奏如左。

translations.literal: Privately I have seen Sima Xiangru and Yang Ziyun compose rhapsodies to admonish the lord above; your subject sincerely admires them, and prostrate I have made one piece of writing, named "On the Capital," respectfully submitting it sealed as follows on the left.
translations.idiomatic: I have watched Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong write fu to counsel their sovereigns; in humble emulation I have drafted a piece called "On the Capital," which I respectfully enclose herewith.

sentences.zh: 皇帝以建武十八年二月甲辰，升舆洛邑，巡于西岳。

translations.literal: The emperor, on the jiachen day of the second month in the eighteenth year of Jianwu, ascended his carriage at Luoyang and toured to the western marchmount.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighteenth year of Jianwu, on the day jiachen of the second month, the emperor left Luoyuan in his carriage and journeyed west toward the sacred peak.

sentences.zh: 推天时，顺斗极，排阊阖，入函谷，观厄于崤、黾，图险于陇、蜀。

translations.literal: He pushed the patterns of heaven, complied with the Dipper's pivot, pushed aside the Gate of Heaven, entered Hangu Pass, observed the narrows at Xiao and Mian, and charted the defiles of Long and Shu.
translations.idiomatic: He read the celestial signs, followed the Pole Star, passed through the celestial gate, entered Hangu, surveyed the Xiao and Mian defiles, and took the measure of the Long and Shu fastnesses.

translations.literal: In that month on the day dingyou he traveled and arrived at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: That same month, on dingyou, he reached Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 经营宫室，伤愍旧京，即诏京兆，乃命扶风，斋肃致敬，告觐园陵。

translations.literal: He planned and managed the palace buildings, was wounded and grieved for the old capital, immediately issued edicts to the capital region and then ordered Feng to fast and purify and show reverence, announcing his visit to the imperial tombs.
translations.idiomatic: He inspected the palace works, mourned the fallen glory of the old capital, and at once commanded the metropolitan prefect and the governor of Feng to observe ritual purity and pay formal visit to the mausoleum parks.

sentences.zh: 凄然有怀祖之思，喟乎以思诸夏之隆。

translations.literal: Sorrowfully he harbored thoughts of his ancestors; sighing, he pondered the greatness of the Xia heartland.
translations.idiomatic: His heart filled with sorrow for the ancestors he had never seen; he sighed over the grandeur that had once been All-under-Heaven's center.

sentences.zh: 遂天旋云游，造舟于渭，北<方亢>泾流。

translations.literal: Then heaven turned and clouds roamed; he built boats on the Wei and bore north along the current of the Jing.
translations.idiomatic: Then the court wheeled like heaven's pivot and drifted like clouds: boats were launched on the Wei and the flotilla pressed north along the Jing's stream.

sentences.zh: 千乘方毂，万骑骈罗，衍陈于岐、梁，东横乎大河。

translations.literal: A thousand chariots in squared hub-lines, ten thousand riders ranged side by side; they spread formations at Qi and Liang and stretched east across the great river.
translations.idiomatic: A thousand chariots ran hub to hub, ten thousand horsemen filled the roads; battle lines stretched from Qi and Liang eastward across the Yellow River.

translations.literal: He buried offerings to Hou Tu and performed the suburban sacrifice.
translations.idiomatic: He buried jade for the earth god at the suburban altar and offered the prescribed rites at the round-mound sacrifice.

translations.literal: In that year, in the fourth month, he returned to the Luoyang capital.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth month of that year he was back in the capital at Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 明年，有诏复函谷关，作大驾宫、六王邸、高车厩于长安。

translations.literal: The next year there was an edict to restore Hangu Pass, and to build the Grand Procession Palace, the lodges of the six kings, and the tall-chariot stables at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: The following year an edict reopened Hangu Pass and ordered the Grand Procession Palace, the six princes' hostels, and the tall-wheeled carriage stables rebuilt at Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 修理东都城门，桥泾、渭，往往缮离观。

translations.literal: He repaired the eastern capital's city gates, bridged the Jing and Wei, and here and there repaired detached belvederes.
translations.idiomatic: The eastern capital's gates were repaired, bridges thrown across the Jing and Wei, and scattered lookout towers restored along the way.

sentences.zh: 东临霸、浐，西望昆明，北登长平，规龙首，抚未央，覛平乐，仪建章。

translations.literal: East he overlooked Ba and Chan; west he gazed on Kunming; north he ascended Changping; he traced Dragon Head, stroked Weiyang, surveyed Pingle, and took measure of Jianzhang.
translations.idiomatic: To the east he looked down on the Ba and Chan streams; to the west his eye fell on Kunming Pool; to the north he climbed Changping, traced Dragon Head Ridge, paced Weiyang Palace, scanned Pingle Lodge, and took in Jianzhang Hall.

sentences.zh: 是时山东翕然狐疑，意圣朝之西都， 惧关门之反拒也。

translations.literal: At this time east of the mountains there was a sudden fox-like wavering; they suspected the sage court's western capital and feared the passes' gates would be shut against them.
translations.idiomatic: Then the eastern provinces buzzed with unease, wondering whether the court meant to stay in the western capital and fearing that the inner passes might be closed in their faces.

sentences.zh: 客有为笃言：“彼□井之潢污，固不容夫吞舟；

translations.literal: A guest spoke to Du, saying: "That puddle of a dry well's ditch, of course cannot accommodate one who would swallow a boat.
translations.idiomatic: A visitor said to Du Du: "A roadside puddle beside a dried-up well cannot float a vessel meant to swallow the sea."

sentences.zh: 且洛邑之渟瀯，曷足以居乎万乘哉？

translations.literal: Moreover Luoyang's stagnant pool—how could it suffice to house the ten thousand chariots?
translations.idiomatic: As for Luoyang's shallow basin, how could it hold an empire of ten thousand chariots?"

sentences.zh: 咸阳守国利器，不可久虚，以示奸萌。

translations.literal: Xianyang is the sharp weapon for guarding the state; it cannot long be left empty to show treacherous sprouts the way.
translations.idiomatic: Xianyang is the keen blade of dynastic defense; leave it vacant too long and you only invite schemers to test the edge."

sentences.zh: ”笃未甚然其言也，故因为述大汉之崇，世据雍州之利，而今国家未暇之故，以喻客意。

translations.literal: " Du was not greatly persuaded by these words; therefore on account of this he set forth the loftiness of the great Han, how generation after generation relied on the advantages of Yongzhou, and how now the state had not yet had leisure, in order to instruct the guest's intent.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du was not wholly convinced; he therefore laid out the majesty of the Han, its long reliance on Yongzhou's strength, and the exigencies that now kept the court from a full return west—meant to answer his visitor's doubts.

translations.literal: He said:
translations.idiomatic: He said:

sentences.zh: 昔在强秦，爰初开畔，霸自岐、雍，国富人衍，卒以并兼，桀虐作乱。

translations.literal: In the past, when mighty Qin first opened its borders, hegemony rose from Qi and Yong; the state was rich and the people abundant, and in the end they annexed all; Jie-like cruelty arose in disorder.
translations.idiomatic: When all-powerful Qin first carved out its realm, hegemonic power rose from Qi and Yong; the land grew rich and populous until Qin swallowed every rival—then tyranny like Jie's provoked rebellion.

translations.literal: Heaven's mandate had a sage; it entrusted it to the great Han.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven reserved its mandate for a sage and laid it on the great Han.

translations.literal: The great Han opened its foundation; the high ancestor had merit.
translations.idiomatic: The Han founded its line, and the High Ancestor bore the chief merit.

sentences.zh: 斩白蛇，屯黑云，聚五星于东井，提干将而呵暴秦。

translations.literal: He cut the white serpent, halted under black clouds, gathered the five planets at the Eastern Well, raised the keen sword and shouted down violent Qin.
translations.idiomatic: He slew the white serpent, camped beneath black clouds, watched the five planets cluster over the Eastern Well, raised his keen blade, and roared defiance at brutal Qin.

sentences.zh: 蹈沧海，跨昆仑，奋彗光，扫项军，遂济人难，荡涤于泗、沂。

translations.literal: He trod the deep sea, leapt Kunlun, brandished comet light, swept Xiang Yu's army, then delivered men from disaster and washed away chaos on the Si and Yi.
translations.idiomatic: He crossed the eastern sea, vaulted Kunlun, flashed like a comet's tail, shattered Xiang Yu's host, rescued the people from calamity, and rinsed the land clean along the Si and Yi.

translations.literal: Liu Jing proposed the plan; at first they capitalled at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Jing framed the strategy, and the capital was first fixed at Chang'an.

translations.literal: The August Ancestor received the flowing current and guarded it with culture.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen took up that legacy and preserved it through humane government.

sentences.zh: 躬履节俭，侧身行仁，食不二味，衣无异采。

translations.literal: Personally he practiced frugality; he inclined his body to enact benevolence; he did not eat two flavors, and his clothes had no varied colors.
translations.idiomatic: He lived plainly, bent every effort to kindness, took no second dish at meals, and wore no gaudy silks.

sentences.zh: 赈人以农桑，率下以约已，曼丽之容不悦于目，郑、卫之声不过于耳，佞邪之臣不列于朝，巧伪之物不鬻于市，故能理升平而刑几措。

translations.literal: He relieved the people through farming and sericulture; he led those below by restraining himself; sumptuous beauty did not please his eyes, the sounds of Zheng and Wei did not pass his ears, fawning evil ministers did not stand in his court, cunning false goods were not sold in his markets; therefore he was able to order rising peace and punishments nearly ceased.
translations.idiomatic: He succored the people with tillage and silk, taught restraint by his own example, turned from sensual beauty, shut his ears to the licentious music of Zheng and Wei, kept sycophants from his hall, and banned shoddy wares from the market—so that an age of peace rose and the racks of punishment stood almost empty.

sentences.zh: 富衍于孝、景，功传于后嗣。

translations.literal: Wealth overflowed under Filial Emperors Xiao and Jing; merit was transmitted to later heirs.
translations.idiomatic: Wealth swelled under Emperors Jing and his father; their achievement passed down the line.

sentences.zh: 是时，孝武因其余财府帑之蓄，始有钩深图远之意，探冒顿之罪，校平城之仇。

translations.literal: At this time, Filial Wu, relying on the remainder wealth and treasury stores, first had the intention to plumb the deep and plan the far; he investigated Modun's crimes and compared Pingcheng's grudge.
translations.idiomatic: Then Emperor Wu, drawing on accumulated treasure in the vaults, first conceived designs on distant horizons: he would reckon Modun's offenses and avenge the humiliation at Pingcheng.

sentences.zh: 遂命票骑，勤任卫青，勇惟鹰扬，军如流星，深之匈奴，割裂王庭，席卷漠北，叩勒祁连，横分单于，屠裂百蛮。

translations.literal: Thereupon he ordered the Swift Cavalry, diligently employed Wei Qing; courage was only like the hawk's soar; armies were like meteors; they went deep into the Xiongnu, carved apart the kingly court, rolled up the northern desert, knocked at Qilian, split the Chanyu crosswise, slaughtered and tore the hundred barbarians.
translations.idiomatic: He summoned the Swift Cavalry, gave Wei Qing heavy responsibility, and sent armies shooting like meteors deep into the steppe: they shattered the royal court, swept the northern sands, stormed the Qilian range, cut the Chanyu in two, and butchered countless tribes.

sentences.zh: 烧罽帐，系阏氏，燔康居，灰珍奇，椎鸣镝，钉鹿蠡，驰坑岸，获昆弥，虏亻数侲，驱骡驴，御宛马，鞭□騠。

translations.literal: They burned felt tents, bound the queen, burned Kangju, turned treasures to ash, hammered whistling arrows, pinned the Lu-li, raced the pit banks, captured the Kunmi, took youthful captives, drove mules and donkeys, rode Ferghana horses, lashed the swift coursers.
translations.idiomatic: They torched the felt yurts, seized the khatun, put Kangju to the flame, reduced rarities to ash, smashed whistling arrows, pinned the Lu-li chieftain, charged the gully lines, seized the Kunmi ruler, drove off herds of pack animals, mounted blood-sweating horses from Ferghana, and whipped on the fleet coursers.

translations.literal: They expanded territory ten thousand li; might shook the eight wilds.
translations.idiomatic: They pushed the frontier ten thousand li; their majesty shook the eight outer regions.

translations.literal: They first established four commanderies and held Dunhuang.
translations.idiomatic: They founded the four western commanderies and planted a garrison at Dunhuang.

translations.literal: They merged border dependent states; one commandery held the western regions.
translations.idiomatic: They folded dependent states into the border and let a single commandery oversee the Western Regions.

translations.literal: They set marquises on the northern corner and established the Protector of the Western Qiang.
translations.idiomatic: They planted marquises on the northern marches and created the office of Protector of the Western Qiang.

translations.literal: They drove the Di and Bo, made sparse the wolves of Qiong and Zuo.
translations.idiomatic: They drove the Di and Bo peoples, and thinned the wolfish bands of Qiong and Zuo.

translations.literal: East they rubbed the Wuhuan, trampled the Hui and Mo.
translations.idiomatic: To the east they brushed the Wuhuan and trampled the Hui and Mo tribes.

translations.literal: South they bridled Gou Ding, crossed swords on the mighty Yue.
translations.idiomatic: To the south they haltered Gou Ding and crossed blades with defiant Yue.

translations.literal: They mutilated the tattooed barbarians; sea waves foamed with blood.
translations.idiomatic: They broke the tattooed southerners until the sea foamed red.

translations.literal: Commanderies and counties reached Rinan; they floated rafts to Zhuya.
translations.idiomatic: County government ran south to Rinan; rafts bore the army's awe to Zhuya.

translations.literal: The commandant's posts reached the southeast; they also held Huangzhi.
translations.idiomatic: Southeastern outposts of the commandant reached even Huangzhi.

sentences.zh: 连缓耳，琐雕题，摧天督，牵象犀，椎蚌蛤，碎琉璃，甲玳瑁，戕觜觿。

translations.literal: They linked the pendant-eared, locked the carved-forehead, crushed the celestial supervisor, led elephants and rhinos, hammered clams, shattered colored glass, shelled tortoiseshell, broke the rhinoceros gores.
translations.idiomatic: They chained the long-eared envoys, collared the tattoo-browed chiefs, broke the "celestial duke," led off elephants and rhinos, smashed pearl shells and glassware, cracked tortoise carapaces and rhino-horn hilts.

sentences.zh: 于是同穴裘褐之域，共川鼻饮之国，莫不袒跣稽颡，失气虏伏。

translations.literal: Thereupon in regions of same-burrow fur-cloth and lands of shared-river nose-drinking, none did not bare feet and knock foreheads, lose breath and lie prostrate in submission.
translations.idiomatic: Then every land of fur-clad cave-dwellers and every tribe that drank from a common stream bared their feet, pressed brow to dust, and lay breathless in surrender.

sentences.zh: 非夫大汉之世盛，世借雍土之饶，得御外理内之术，孰能致功若斯！

translations.literal: If it were not for the great Han's age of splendor, generation after generation borrowing the abundance of Yong soil, obtaining the arts of governing within and ordering without—who could have achieved merit like this!
translations.idiomatic: Had not the Han reached such zenith, generation on generation drawing on Yongzhou's fat soil and wielding arts of inner rule and outer command, who could have wrought feats like these?"

sentences.zh: 故创业于高祖，嗣传于孝惠，德隆于太宗，财衍于孝景，威盛于圣武，政行于宣、元，侈极于成、哀、祚缺于孝平。

translations.literal: Therefore the enterprise was founded with the high ancestor, the succession transmitted under Filial Hui, virtue rose under the August Ancestor, wealth overflowed under Filial Jing, might flourished under the sage martial emperor, government ran under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, extravagance reached its limit under Cheng, Ai, and the mandate broke under Filial Ping.
translations.idiomatic: The line began with the High Ancestor, passed through Emperor Hui, rose in virtue under Emperor Wen, swelled in wealth under Emperor Jing, blazed in might under Emperor Wu, ran smoothly under Emperors Xuan and Yuan, sank into excess under Cheng and Ai, and snapped under the boy Emperor Ping.

sentences.zh: 传世十一，历载三百，德衰而复盈，道微而复章，皆莫能迁于雍州，而背于咸阳。

translations.literal: Eleven generations were transmitted, passing three hundred years; virtue declined then filled again, the way grew faint then shone again; yet none could shift from Yongzhou or turn their back on Xianyang.
translations.idiomatic: Eleven reigns spanned three hundred years: virtue waned and waxed, the Way dimmed and brightened—yet none ever thought to abandon Yongzhou or turn away from Xianyang.

sentences.zh: 宫室寝庙，山陵相望，高显弘丽，可思可荣，羲、农已来，无兹著明。

translations.literal: Palace chambers and temple shrines, mountain tombs gazing at one another, high, manifest, vast, and splendid—thinkable and glorious—since Fu Xi and Shen Nong, none has been thus illustrious.
translations.idiomatic: Palaces and shrines, imperial tumuli shoulder to shoulder—lofty, bright, vast, glorious—since the age of Fu Xi and Shen Nong nothing has matched their splendor.

sentences.zh: 夫雍州本帝皇所以育业、霸王所以衍功，战士角难之场也。

translations.literal: Now Yongzhou is fundamentally where the emperors nurtured their enterprise and hegemons extended their merit; it is the ground where warriors strove in difficulty.
translations.idiomatic: Yongzhou is where emperors reared dynastic foundations and hegemons piled up achievement; it is the very arena where soldiers proved their mettle.

translations.literal: What the "Tribute of Yu" records, its fields were rated highest.
translations.idiomatic: The "Tribute of Yu" ranks its soil the finest grade.

translations.literal: Fertile wilds stretch a thousand li; plains and low marshes fill the eye.
translations.idiomatic: A thousand li of fertile plain roll away; marsh and bottomland stretch to the horizon.

translations.literal: It preserves and grows the five grains; mulberry and hemp flourish in orderly profusion.
translations.idiomatic: The five grains thrive in abundance; mulberry and hemp grow in luxuriant rows.

sentences.zh: 滨据南山，带以泾、渭，号曰陆海，蠢生万类。

translations.literal: It borders and leans on the southern mountains, is girded by the Jing and Wei, is called the dry land sea; stupid life of the myriad kinds.
translations.idiomatic: It hugs the southern ranges and is belted by the Jing and Wei—what men call the "inland sea," teeming with every kind of creature.

translations.literal: Pian-nan, tan, and zhe; fruits and vegetables ripen to fruit.
translations.idiomatic: Piannan, sandalwood, and zhe timber flourish; orchards and kitchen gardens bear heavy fruit.

sentences.zh: 畎渎润淤，水泉灌溉，渐泽成川，粳稻陶遂。

translations.literal: Ditches and drains soak the silt; water springs irrigate; gradually the marshes become rivers; glutinous and non-glutinous rice thrive in ease.
translations.idiomatic: Irrigation channels leach the silt, springs water the fields, marshes widen into streams, and both sticky and ordinary rice flourish without strain.

translations.literal: The ointment of its soil: the price of a mu is one gold.
translations.idiomatic: The soil is so rich that a single mu once fetched a full ounce of gold.

translations.literal: Field upon field like each other; hoes and mattocks in the groves.
translations.idiomatic: Plot matches plot in endless green; hoes and mattocks flash among the groves.

translations.literal: Fire ploughing and drifting seed; shallow labor, deep gain.
translations.idiomatic: Slash-and-burn and broadcast sowing yield ample harvests for modest toil.

sentences.zh: 既有蓄积，厄塞四临：四被陇、蜀，南通汉中，北据谷口，东阻嵚岩。

translations.literal: Once there are stores piled up, perilous barriers close on four sides: on four sides embraced by Long and Shu, south connecting to Hanzhong, north occupying Gukou, east blocked by sheer crags.
translations.idiomatic: With granaries full, four sides are sealed by natural ramparts: Long and Shu fold round it, Hanzhong opens to the south, Gukou bars the north, and precipitous cliffs choke the east.

translations.literal: Hangu Pass guards the heights; the road east of the mountains ends.
translations.idiomatic: Hangu's gate commands the heights; east of the mountains the road simply stops.

translations.literal: Set lines at Qian and Long; choke and lie down the western Rong.
translations.idiomatic: Lines of defense on Qian and Long stifle the western Rong.

translations.literal: Hold Bao and Xie; south of the ranges there is no passage.
translations.idiomatic: Hold the Bao and Xie defiles and nothing crosses the southern ranges.

translations.literal: Stop the mouth and cut the fords; the northern deserts have no route from which to come.
translations.idiomatic: Seal the passes and break the ferries, and the northern steppe has no way in.

translations.literal: The currents of Hong and Wei flow straight into the Yellow River.
translations.idiomatic: The Hong and Wei pour straight into the Yellow River.

translations.literal: Great ships in myriads; transport grain passes one another.
translations.idiomatic: Ten thousand great barges ply the channels, grain convoys passing hull to hull.

translations.literal: East they bind the dark sea; west they net the flowing sands.
translations.idiomatic: To the east they rope in the dark sea; to the west they net the drifting sands.

translations.literal: South of the north and sound of harmony, the various Xia are at peace.
translations.idiomatic: From the northern marches to the southern coasts a single harmony reigns; the Hua heartland rests at peace.

translations.literal: City walls a hundred feet; narrows and passes are critical points.
translations.idiomatic: City walls rise a hundred feet; every defile marks a choke point.

translations.literal: The perils of passes and bridges: many places are belt-girdled.
translations.idiomatic: Bridges and mountain gates pinch the roads like a belt drawn tight.

translations.literal: One soldier raises a catapult stone; a thousand men are sunk in delay.
translations.idiomatic: One man working a traction-trebuchet can bog a thousand attackers in the mud.

translations.literal: One man wields a halberd; three armies are defeated in spirit.
translations.idiomatic: A single halberdier on the wall can break an army's nerve.

sentences.zh: 地势便利，介胄剽悍，可与守近，利以攻远。

translations.literal: Terrain and position are convenient; armor and helmet are fierce; one may with them guard what is near and profit to attack what is far.
translations.idiomatic: The ground favors the defender and the men wear fierce mail: you can hold the near at ease and strike the far with advantage.

translations.literal: Soldiers are easy to protect; men do not bare their flesh.
translations.idiomatic: Troops find cover readily; no warrior need fight stripped to the skin.

translations.literal: Beginning twelve, this is called rich fat.
translations.idiomatic: Twelve such districts form what men call the empire's fattest pasture.

sentences.zh: 用霸则兼并，先据则功殊；

translations.literal: Using hegemony then annexing; first occupying then merit is different.
translations.idiomatic: Use hegemonic force and you annex rivals; seize the ground first and your achievement is unmatched.

sentences.zh: 修文则财衍，行武则士要；

translations.literal: Cultivating culture then wealth overflows; practicing martial affairs then knights are essential.
translations.idiomatic: Pursue civil arts and wealth multiplies; train warriors and bold knights flock to you.

sentences.zh: 为政则化上，篡逆则难诛；

translations.literal: Ordering government then transformation rises above; usurpation and rebellion then are hard to execute.
translations.idiomatic: Rule uprightly and the people look upward in trust; would-be usurpers find no opening.

sentences.zh: 进攻则百克，退守则有余：斯固帝王之渊囿，而守国之利器也。

translations.literal: Attack then a hundred victories; defend then there is surplus: this is indeed the imperial park of emperors and the sharp weapon for guarding the state.
translations.idiomatic: Attack and you win every clash; defend and your stores overflow—such is the emperor's walled park and the keen blade of dynastic defense.

sentences.zh: 逮及亡新，时汉之衰，偷忍渊囿，篡器慢违，徒以势便，莫能卒危。

translations.literal: Reaching to the perished Xin, at the time of Han's decline, they stole endurance in the imperial park, usurped the vessels and were slow and contrary; relying only on positional convenience, none could in the end bring danger.
translations.idiomatic: Even when Xin usurped the throne at Han's ebb, Wang Mang slunk within those same royal preserves, seized the regalia, and grew arrogant—yet for all his positional advantage he could not in the end avert ruin."

translations.literal: The usurper's eighteen years ended in execution at the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Mang's eighteen-year reign collapsed when he was put to death in the capital.

translations.literal: Heaven bestowed Gengshi, yet he could not hold the reins.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven raised the Gengshi emperor, but he could not keep the realm in hand.

translations.literal: Careless hoarding invited bandits, and again brought the Red Eyebrows.
translations.idiomatic: Loose guarding of the treasury drew marauders, and the Red Eyebrows rose in turn.

translations.literal: Within the seas it was cloud-wrack and turmoil; the central states were nearly snuffed out.
translations.idiomatic: The empire boiled like storm clouds; the heartland of the Xia almost perished.

translations.literal: Many dragons fought at once; none could tell right from wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Rival warlords clawed like dragons in a single pool; no one knew which cause was just.

sentences.zh: 于时圣帝，赫然申威，荷天人之符，兼不世之姿。

translations.literal: Then the sage emperor, in awful majesty, displayed his might; he bore the tally of Heaven and man and united a bearing not seen in generations.
translations.idiomatic: Then our sage sovereign blazed forth in wrath, bore Heaven's mandate and men's hopes, and combined a presence unmatched in his age.

sentences.zh: 受命于皇上，获助于灵祇。

translations.literal: He received the charge from High Heaven and gained aid from the numinous powers.
translations.idiomatic: High Heaven entrusted him with rule, and the spirits of land and altar rallied to his side.

translations.literal: He raised his title at Gaoyi and planted his banners on every front.
translations.idiomatic: He proclaimed his reign at Gaoyi and unfurled the royal ensigns to the four quarters.

translations.literal: The ministers who first framed strategy planned within the curtain and produced the unexpected.
translations.idiomatic: The counselors who first laid the plan plotted behind the screen and struck where no foe expected.

translations.literal: Troops roaring with tiger fury.
translations.idiomatic: Armies snarled like tigers unleashed.

translations.literal: Like tigers, like hornless dragons.
translations.idiomatic: They fought like tigers and hornless dragons—no force could stand before them.

translations.literal: Wherever the host was directed, nothing was not torn asunder.
translations.idiomatic: Every column he aimed swept all before it like a scythe.

sentences.zh: 盖夫燔鱼剸蛇，莫之方斯。

translations.literal: As for burning fish and slicing snakes, none could match this.
translations.idiomatic: They say Qin Shi burned the sacred fish and carved the divine serpent—no tale of old outshone this feat.

translations.literal: A great cry east of the mountains; the echo shook the drifting sands.
translations.idiomatic: His shout rolled from Shandong to the western wastes until the sands trembled.

sentences.zh: 要龙渊，首镆铘，命腾太白，亲发狼、弧。

translations.literal: He girded the Longyuan blade, crowned his host with Mo Ye; he bade the Grand White star leap; with his own hand he drew the Wolf and Archer bows.
translations.idiomatic: He belted the sword Longyuan, brandished Mo Ye, read the omen of Venus at dawn, and himself bent the Wolf- and Archer-star bows.

sentences.zh: 南禽公孙，北背强胡，西平陇、冀，东据洛都。

translations.literal: South he took Gongsun captive; north he turned back the mighty Hu; west he pacified Long and Ji; east he seized the Luoyang capital.
translations.idiomatic: To the south he caged Gongsun Shu, to the north he threw back the Xiongnu, to the west he stilled Long and Ji, to the east he planted the standard at Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 乃廓平帝宇，济蒸人于涂炭，成兆庶之□，遂兴复乎大汉。

translations.literal: Thereupon he cleared the imperial demesne, delivered the steaming masses from mud and charcoal, secured the myriad common people in their welfare, and thus revived the great Han.
translations.idiomatic: He swept the realm clean, snatched the people from fire and mire, gave the myriad households a footing again, and raised the great Han from its ashes.

sentences.zh: 今天下新定，矢石之勤始瘳，而主上方以边垂为忧，忿葭萌之不柔，未遑于论都而遗思雍州也。

translations.literal: Now the realm is newly settled; the toll of arrows and stones has just begun to heal; yet the ruler above still frets the border marches, resents Jiameng's failure to submit, and has no leisure to debate the capital or set aside thought of Yongzhou.
translations.idiomatic: The empire is only just pacified and the wounds of war still closing, yet His Majesty's mind runs first to the frontiers, to stubborn Jiameng in the west; he has no spare moment to argue capitals or to forget the old seat in Yongzhou.

sentences.zh: 方躬劳圣思，以率海内，厉抚名将，略地疆外，信威于征伐，展武乎荒裔。

translations.literal: Just now he personally exhausts sacred thought to lead all within the seas, vigorously comforts famous generals, seizes ground beyond the borders, extends trust and might through punitive expeditions, and displays martial power in the wild outer marches.
translations.idiomatic: He bends his own person to guide the realm, heartens his best commanders, pushes the frontier outward, lets campaign after campaign speak his authority, and shows the flag in the farthest barbarian lands.

sentences.zh: 若夫文身鼻饮缓耳之主，椎结左衽□鍝之君，东南殊俗不羁之国，西北绝域难制之邻，靡不重译纳贡，请为籓臣。

translations.literal: As for rulers with tattooed bodies, nose-drinking, and pendant ears, and chiefs with topknots, left-lapelled coats, and metal rings—lands of alien custom in the southeast that will not be bridled, neighbors in unreachable wastes of the northwest hard to control—none failed to send relay interpreters with tribute and beg to become vassal ministers.
translations.idiomatic: Whether tattooed nose-drinking chiefs with weighted earlobes, or topknotted left-lapped lords with bronze rings at the belt—southern tribes beyond our law, northwestern peoples beyond easy reach—all sent envoys through double translation, laden with gifts, suing to be Han vassals.

translations.literal: The sovereign still declined modestly and did not boast of his labors.
translations.idiomatic: Yet the emperor still answered with modest demurral and refused to trumpet his own toil.

sentences.zh: 意以为获无用之虏，不如安有益之民；

translations.literal: His mind held that to take useless captives is not as good as settling a people who can profit the state.
translations.idiomatic: He judged that dragging home useless prisoners was poorer policy than cherishing citizens who could enrich the realm.

sentences.zh: 略荒裔之地，不如保殖五谷之渊；

translations.literal: To seize tracts in wild borderlands is not as good as preserving and multiplying the granary of the five grains.
translations.idiomatic: Snatching barren steppe was less wise than tending the deep breadbasket of the central plain.

sentences.zh: 远救于已亡，不若近而存存也。

translations.literal: To rescue from afar what is already lost is not as good as keeping close at hand what still endures.
translations.idiomatic: To chase ghosts beyond the frontier was folly when the living heartland still needed care.

sentences.zh: 今国家躬修道德，吐惠含仁，湛恩沾洽，时风显宣。

translations.literal: Now the court personally cultivates virtue and the Way, breathes out kindness and holds benevolence within; its deep favor soaks everywhere, and the timely wind of policy is openly proclaimed.
translations.idiomatic: Today the dynasty walks the path of virtue, speaks in mercy and justice, pours its grace into every corner, and lets honest policy ride on an open wind.

sentences.zh: 徒垂意于持平守实，务在爱育元元，苟有便于王政者，圣主纳焉。

translations.literal: It bends its mind only to holding the balance and guarding substance, strives to love and nurture the black-haired people; if anything serves royal government, the sage ruler adopts it.
translations.idiomatic: It cares chiefly for even-handed rule and plain dealing, for feeding and fathering the common folk; whatever truly serves good government, the sage throne accepts.

translations.literal: Why is this?
translations.idiomatic: Why so?

sentences.zh: 物罔挹而不损，道无隆而不移，阳盛则运，阴满则亏，故存不忘亡，安不讳危，虽有仁义，犹设城池也。

translations.literal: Of things none is drawn without diminution; of the Way none rises high without shifting; when yang flourishes it moves, when yin fills it wanes; therefore while surviving forget not perishing, in peace do not shun speaking of danger; even though there are benevolence and right, still one sets city walls and moats.
translations.idiomatic: Nothing taken from the common stock fails to diminish the whole; no way climbs forever without turning; yang at its height must roll onward, yin at the full must ebb—hence the wise remember ruin in the hour of success and speak of peril in times of calm; even under humane rule, walls and gates remain needful.

sentences.zh: 客以利器不可久虚，而国家亦不忘乎西都，何必去洛邑之渟瀯与？

translations.literal: The guest holds that the sharp weapon cannot long stand empty, yet the state also does not forget the western capital—why then must one abandon Luoyang's pools?
translations.idiomatic: Your visitor says Xianyang must not lie open to intrigue—true enough—yet the court has not forgotten the western capital either; need that mean forsaking Luoyang's deeper basin?

translations.literal: Later Du served as literary aide in the commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du later held the post of literary clerk in his commandery.

sentences.zh: 以目疾，二十余年不窥京师。

translations.literal: Because of an eye ailment, for more than twenty years he did not look upon the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Eye trouble kept him from the capital for over twenty years.

sentences.zh: 笃之外高祖破羌将军辛武贤，以武略称。

translations.literal: Du's great-grandfather on his mother's side was the Qiang-Smashing General Xin Wuxian, famed for martial strategy.
translations.idiomatic: On his mother's side he counted the "Qiang-Smashing" general Xin Wuxian, celebrated for military stratagem.

sentences.zh: 笃常叹曰：“杜氏文明善政，而笃不任为吏；

translations.literal: Du often sighed, saying: "The Du line were civil, enlightened, and good in government, yet I am not fit to be an official.
translations.idiomatic: Du Du would sigh: "The Dus were lettered men who governed well, yet I am no good as an administrator.

sentences.zh: 辛氏秉义经武，而笃又怯于事。

translations.literal: The Xin clan upheld righteousness and managed arms, yet I am also timid in affairs.
translations.idiomatic: The Xins bore arms in a just cause, yet I am too timid for such work.

translations.literal: For five generations on both sides, down to me Du, decline has come!"
translations.idiomatic: Five generations of worth on either side—and it ends in me, a cipher!

translations.literal: His younger sister married into the Ma clan of Fufeng.
translations.idiomatic: A younger sister wedded into the prominent Ma family of Fufeng.

sentences.zh: 建初三年，车骑将军马防击西羌，请笃为从事中郎，战没于射姑山。

translations.literal: In the third year of Jianchu, the chariot-and-horse general Ma Fang attacked the Western Qiang and invited Du as attendant clerk in the headquarters staff; he died in battle at Mount Shegu.
translations.idiomatic: In Jianchu 3 the chariot-and-cavalry general Ma Fang campaigned against the western Qiang and took Du Du on staff as an attendant clerk; Du fell fighting at Mount Shegu.

sentences.zh: 所著赋、诔、吊、书、赞、《七言》、《女诫》及杂文，凡十八篇。

translations.literal: What he authored—fu, dirges, condolences, letters, encomia, "In Seven Lines," "Admonitions for Women," and miscellaneous pieces—totals eighteen works.
translations.idiomatic: His writings—rhapsodies, laments, elegies, letters, praises, the verse cycle "Seven Lines," the "Admonitions for Women," and miscellanea—come to eighteen titles.

translations.literal: He also wrote "Disquisitions on a Bright Age" in fifteen sections.
translations.idiomatic: He also composed the "Disquisitions on a Luminous Age" in fifteen chapters.

translations.literal: His son Shuo was chivalrous and bold, and became known for trade and enrichment.
translations.idiomatic: His son Shuo was a swaggering knight-errant who made a name in commerce.

sentences.zh: 王隆字文山，冯翊云阳人也。

translations.literal: Wang Long, courtesy name Wenshan, was a man of Yunyang in Pingyi.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Long, whose courtesy name was Wenshan, came from Yunyang in Pingyi commandery.

sentences.zh: 王莽时，以父任为郎，后避难河西，为窦融左护军。

translations.literal: Under Wang Mang, by his father's privilege he became a gentleman; later he fled troubles to Hexi and became Dou Rong's left protector general.
translations.idiomatic: Under Wang Mang he entered office through his father's rank; when chaos came he took refuge west of the Yellow River and served Dou Rong as left protector general.

translations.literal: In the Jianwu era he became magistrate of Xinji.
translations.idiomatic: During the Jianwu reign he was appointed magistrate of Xinji.

sentences.zh: 能文章，所著诗、赋、铭、书凡二十六篇。

translations.literal: He was capable in letters; what he authored—poems, fu, inscriptions, and letters—totals twenty-six pieces.
translations.idiomatic: He was a skilled writer; his poems, rhapsodies, inscriptions, and letters number twenty-six pieces.

sentences.zh: 初，王莽末，沛国史岑子孝亦以文章显，莽以为谒者，著颂、诔、《复神》、《说疾》凡四篇。

translations.literal: Earlier, at the end of Wang Mang, Shi Cen, courtesy name Zixiao, of the Pei kingdom was also distinguished in letters; Mang made him a receptionist; he authored odes, dirges, "Return of the Spirits," and "On Illness"—four works in all.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, in Wang Mang's last days, Shi Cen (Zixiao) of Pei won fame as a man of letters; Mang named him court herald, and he left four works—odes, laments, "Return of the Spirits," and "On Illness."

sentences.zh: 夏恭字敬公，梁国蒙人也。

translations.literal: Xia Gong, courtesy name Jinggong, was a man of Meng in the Liang state.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Gong, courtesy name Jinggong, was a native of Meng in the kingdom of Liang.

sentences.zh: 习《韩诗》、《孟氏易》，讲授门徒常千余人。

translations.literal: He studied the Han version of the Odes and Meng's Changes, and when he lectured his disciples were always over a thousand.
translations.idiomatic: He mastered the Han-school Odes and the Meng commentary on the Changes, and his lecture hall regularly held more than a thousand students.

sentences.zh: 王莽末，盗贼从横，攻没郡县。

translations.literal: At the end of Wang Mang, bandits swarmed unchecked and attacked and overthrew commanderies and counties.
translations.idiomatic: In the final years of Wang Mang, rebels ran riot and overran whole districts.

sentences.zh: 恭以恩信为众所附，拥兵固守，独安全。

translations.literal: Gong by kindness and trustworthiness was adhered to by the masses; he held troops and firmly defended, and alone remained wholly secure.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Gong won the people by good faith, kept his garrison intact, and alone among the towns came through unscathed.

sentences.zh: 光武即位，嘉其忠果，召拜郎中，再迁太山都尉。

translations.literal: When Guangwu ascended the throne, he praised Gong's loyalty and resolution, summoned him and appointed gentleman of the interior, and twice promoted him to commandant of Taishan.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Guangwu took the throne he commended Xia's steadfast courage, summoned him as a gentleman of the interior, and twice advanced him to commandant of Taishan.

translations.literal: He harmonized and gathered the common people and greatly won their hearts.
translations.idiomatic: He soothed and rallied the populace until they loved him dearly.

sentences.zh: 恭善为文，著赋、颂、诗、《励学》凡二十篇。

translations.literal: Gong was good at writing; he authored fu, odes, poems, and "Encouragement to Study"—twenty pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: Xia Gong wrote well; his rhapsodies, hymns, poems, and "Encouragement to Study" fill twenty pieces.

sentences.zh: 年四十九卒官，诸儒共谥曰宣明君。

translations.literal: At age forty-nine he died in office; the scholars together gave him the posthumous title Lord Xuanming.
translations.idiomatic: He died in harness at forty-nine, and the literati jointly honored him posthumously as Lord Xuanming.

sentences.zh: 子牙，少习家业，著赋、颂、赞、诔凡四十篇。

translations.literal: His son Ziya in youth studied the family learning and authored fu, odes, encomia, and dirges—forty pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: His son Ziya continued the household scholarship and produced forty pieces of fu, hymns, praises, and laments.

sentences.zh: 举孝廉，早卒，乡人号曰文德先生。

translations.literal: Recommended as filial and incorrupt, he died young; his fellow villagers styled him Master Wende.
translations.idiomatic: Summoned as filial and incorrupt, he died young; the villagers called him Master Wende.

sentences.zh: 傅毅字武仲，扶风茂陵人也。

translations.literal: Fu Yi, courtesy name Wuzhong, was a man of Maoling in Fufeng.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi, courtesy name Wuzhong, came from Maoling in Fufeng.

translations.literal: In youth he studied broadly.
translations.idiomatic: As a youth he read widely.

sentences.zh: 永平中，于平陵习章句，因作《迪志诗》曰：

translations.literal: In the Yongping era, at Pingling he practiced glosses and exegesis, and on that account composed the "Poem of Awakened Purpose," saying:
translations.idiomatic: During Yongping he pursued textual study at Pingling and thereupon wrote his "Poem of Awakened Purpose," which begins:

translations.literal: I address you, many gentlemen: seize the season and strive.
translations.idiomatic: Hear me, you gentlemen: the hour calls for effort.

translations.literal: Sun and moon pass and depart—how can you say they will return!
translations.idiomatic: Sun and moon race on—do you think they wheel back for you?

translations.literal: Pity me in my striving; my strength cannot reach the end.
translations.idiomatic: I pity myself in this striving—my strength will not carry the burden.

translations.literal: Here I am, weak and young, with nowhere to establish myself.
translations.idiomatic: Weak and still young, I have no footing from which to rise.

translations.literal: Oh, majestic our ancestor, who shone in the Yin state.
translations.idiomatic: Splendid was our forebear, who blazed bright in the Yin domain.

translations.literal: Twice he trod the traces of the Regulator of the Balance and was able to magnify their model.
translations.idiomatic: Twice he walked in the footsteps of Yi Yin and magnified that pattern.

translations.literal: Wu Ding raised Shang; Yi was honored chief among the lords.
translations.idiomatic: When Wu Ding revived Shang, the house of Yi ranked first among the great clans.

translations.literal: Thus they became thigh and arm; the myriad regions took their rule from them.
translations.idiomatic: They became the sovereign's right arm; the myriad states looked to their standard.

translations.literal: Age after age they bore virtue down to our illustrious late father.
translations.idiomatic: Generation on generation they bore accumulated virtue down to our glorious father.

translations.literal: He guarded and received pure excellence and continued to cultivate their way.
translations.idiomatic: He cherished pure goodness and carried their Way forward.

sentences.zh: 汉之中叶，俊乂式序，秩彼殷宗，光此勋绪。

translations.literal: At the mid-point of Han, outstanding men were arrayed in order; he matched that Yin house and magnified this line of merit.
translations.idiomatic: In Han's middle years worthies stood in rank; he vied with that Yin lineage and widened this heritage of achievement.

translations.literal: I, the little child, am foul and mean and cannot catch up.
translations.idiomatic: I, a mean stripling, am too base to keep pace.

translations.literal: I fear our generations' glory will from this fall away.
translations.idiomatic: I dread lest the fame of our house slip away from this hour.

translations.literal: Who can cleanse the turbid and clear my washing stream?
translations.idiomatic: Who will rinse the mire and give me clean water again?

translations.literal: Who can brighten the dark and open my childish ignorance?
translations.idiomatic: Who will light the gloom and wake my boyish ignorance?

translations.literal: The former men left instructions; I questioned and they admonished.
translations.idiomatic: The elders left precepts; I asked and they counseled me.

translations.literal: They instructed me in fine tasks and taught me broad learning.
translations.idiomatic: They trained me in worthy pursuits and urged me toward wide learning.

translations.literal: Therefore I led friends and sought these old norms.
translations.idiomatic: So I gathered friends and traced these ancient models.

translations.literal: Through separation and union, morning and night, I hoped not to slacken or err.
translations.idiomatic: Through partings and meetings, dawn to dusk, I strove never to flag or stray.

translations.literal: Orderly are the great plans; they are the net and cord for the multitude of models.
translations.idiomatic: Great designs stand in good order—they are the warp through which lesser patterns run.

translations.literal: Without diligence there is no clarity; without singleness there is no depth.
translations.idiomatic: Without zeal there is no insight; without single-mindedness there is no depth.

sentences.zh: 农夫不怠，越有黍稷，谁能云作，考之居息？

translations.literal: If the farmer does not slacken, he will have millet and glutinous panicled millet—who can say he works the clouds? He examines it in dwelling and rest.
translations.idiomatic: The peasant who never idles will fill his bins with grain—who calls that idle cloud-gazing? He proves it in daily toil and nightly rest.

translations.literal: Two tasks ruin the enterprise; many are the ills of my strength.
translations.idiomatic: Two pursuits at once wreck the work; my strength fails under too many burdens.

translations.literal: Like one who follows the great highway, then there is no limit.
translations.idiomatic: Keep to the broad road and the goal stays within reach.

translations.literal: Two aims never succeed; it only wearies my heart.
translations.idiomatic: Two hearts, two failures—only my mind grows weary.

translations.literal: Like listening to everything at once, then one is muddied in sound.
translations.idiomatic: He who hears every voice at once is lost in noise.

translations.literal: Alas, gentleman, do not forever indulge yourself.
translations.idiomatic: Alas, sir—do not forever seek your ease.

translations.literal: The departing years are like a stream; rarely is there a free day.
translations.idiomatic: The years run like water; leisure is a stranger to man.

translations.literal: On the march I halt again and again—how can there be an end?
translations.idiomatic: The road halts me at every turn—how shall I ever arrive?

translations.literal: Diligently morning and evening, together from beginning to end.
translations.idiomatic: Steady from dawn to dusk, one thread from first step to last.

sentences.zh: 毅以显宗求贤不笃，士多隐处，故作《七激》以为讽。

translations.literal: Yi held that the Manifest Ancestor's search for worthies was not earnest, and many gentlemen hid away; therefore he composed the "Seven Stimuli" as a remonstrance.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi believed Emperor Ming had not sought talent with full zeal, so many scholars kept to the hills; he therefore wrote the "Seven Stimuli" as a satirical prod.

sentences.zh: 建初中，肃宗博召文学之士，以毅为兰台令史，拜郎中，与班固、贾逵共典校书。

translations.literal: In the early Jianchu era, Emperor Suzong broadly summoned men of letters, appointed Yi orchid terrace clerk, promoted him to gentleman of the interior, and with Ban Gu and Jia Kui jointly supervised collation of the books.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Jianchu Emperor Zhang cast a wide net for literati, named Fu Yi clerk of the Orchid Terrace, advanced him to gentleman of the interior, and set him with Ban Gu and Jia Kui to collate the imperial library.

sentences.zh: 毅追美李明皇帝功德最盛，而庙颂未立，乃依《清庙》作《显宗颂》十篇奏之，由是文雅显于朝廷。

translations.literal: Yi, looking back in praise, held that the accomplishments and virtue of the enlightened Ming emperor were the greatest, yet no temple hymn had been erected; therefore, following "The Pure Temple," he composed ten pieces of "Hymn to the Manifest Ancestor" and presented them; on this account his literary elegance was displayed at court.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi, extolling the past, argued that Emperor Ming's merit and virtue surpassed all yet lacked a temple ode; modeling on the "Pure Temple" hymn he wrote ten stanzas of a "Hymn to the Manifest Ancestor" and presented them—whereupon his name for elegant prose rang through the palace.

sentences.zh: 车骑将军马防，外戚尊重，请毅为军司马，待以师友之礼。

translations.literal: The chariot-and-horse general Ma Fang, honored as maternal relative, invited Yi as army marshal and treated him with the rites due teacher and friend.
translations.idiomatic: The chariot-and-cavalry general Ma Fang, powerful as an imperial in-law, took Fu Yi as army marshal and honored him as mentor and companion.

translations.literal: When the Ma clan fell, he was dismissed and returned home.
translations.idiomatic: When the Ma family fell from power, Fu Yi was stripped of office and sent home.

sentences.zh: 永元元年，车骑将军窦宪，复请毅为主记室，崔骃为主簿。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yongyuan, the chariot-and-horse general Dou Xian again invited Yi as chief recorder, with Cui Yin as chief clerk.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongyuan 1 the chariot-and-cavalry general Dou Xian again summoned Fu Yi as chief recorder and Cui Yin as chief clerk.

sentences.zh: 及宪迁大将军，复以毅为司马，班固为中护军。

translations.literal: When Xian was promoted to grand general, again he made Yi marshal and Ban Gu middle protector of the army.
translations.idiomatic: When Dou Xian rose to grand general, he again named Fu Yi marshal and Ban Gu middle protector of the army.

sentences.zh: 宪府文章之盛，冠于当世。

translations.literal: The flowering of letters in Xian's headquarters crowned the age.
translations.idiomatic: The brilliance of belles-lettres in Dou Xian's staff outshone every other house of the day.

sentences.zh: 毅早卒，著诗、赋、诔、颂、祝文、《七激》、连珠凡二十八篇。

translations.literal: Yi died early; he authored poems, fu, dirges, odes, blessing texts, the "Seven Stimuli," and linked pearls—twenty-eight pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yi died young; his poems, rhapsodies, laments, hymns, prayer texts, "Seven Stimuli," and "linked pearls" come to twenty-eight titles.

sentences.zh: 黄香字文强，江夏安陆人也。

translations.literal: Huang Xiang, courtesy name Wenqiang, was a man of Anlu in Jiangxia.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang, courtesy name Wenqiang, was a native of Anlu in Jiangxia commandery.

sentences.zh: 年九岁，失母，思慕憔悴，殆不免丧，乡人称其至孝。

translations.literal: At age nine he lost his mother; he thought of her with longing and grew haggard, nearly unable to survive the mourning; his fellow villagers called him supremely filial.
translations.idiomatic: At nine he lost his mother; grief wasted him until he barely lived through the mourning period, and the villagers hailed him as a paragon of filial devotion.

sentences.zh: 年十二，大守刘护闻而召之，署门下孝子，甚见爱敬。

translations.literal: At age twelve the grand warden Liu Hu heard of him and summoned him, appointing him filial son under his gate, and he was greatly loved and respected.
translations.idiomatic: At twelve the grand administrator Liu Hu heard his fame and summoned him, naming him a filial attendant at his gate; the official doted on him and treated him with honor.

sentences.zh: 香家贫，内无仆妾，躬执苦勤，尽心奉养。

translations.literal: Xiang's family was poor; within there were no servants or concubines; personally he took up bitter toil and with full heart served and supported.
translations.idiomatic: The Huang household was poor—no maids within—so he shouldered every hardship himself and nursed his father with utter devotion.

sentences.zh: 遂博学经典，究精道术，能文章，京师号曰“天下无双江夏黄童”。

translations.literal: Thereupon he was broadly learned in the classics, thoroughly investigated the arts of the Way, was capable in letters, and at the capital they styled him "Under Heaven Without Peer—the Huang Lad of Jiangxia."
translations.idiomatic: He went on to master the canon, probed the arts of the Way, and wrote well; the capital dubbed him "the matchless Huang boy of Jiangxia."

sentences.zh: 初除郎中，元和元年，肃宗诏香诣东观，读所未尝见书。

translations.literal: At first removed as gentleman of the interior; in the first year of Yuanhe, Emperor Suzong ordered Huang Xiang to proceed to the Eastern View and read books he had never seen.
translations.idiomatic: His first appointment was gentleman of the interior; in Yuanhe 1 Emperor Zhang sent Huang Xiang to the Eastern Pavilion to read texts he had never opened before.

sentences.zh: 香后告休，及归京师，时千乘王冠，帝会中山邸，乃诏香殿下，顾谓诸王曰：“此‘天下无双江夏黄童’者也。

translations.literal: Later he reported rest leave, and when he returned to the capital, at the time the Prince of Qiansheng underwent the capping ceremony, the emperor met at the Prince of Zhongshan lodge, then ordered Huang Xiang below the hall, looked back and said to the various princes: "This is the one called 'Under Heaven Without Peer—the Huang Lad of Jiangxia.'"
translations.idiomatic: After a leave Huang Xiang returned to court just as the Prince of Qiansheng came of age; the emperor received the princes at the Prince of Zhongshan residence, called Huang Xiang forward below the dais, and said to his sons, "Here is the 'matchless Huang boy of Jiangxia' they all talk about."

translations.literal: Those left and right none did not change their expression.
translations.idiomatic: Every courtier in earshot sat up straighter and looked at him with new respect.

sentences.zh: 后召诣安福殿言政事，拜尚书郎，数陈得失，赏赉增加。

translations.literal: Later he was summoned to the Anfu Hall to speak on government affairs, was appointed gentleman of the masters of writing, repeatedly stated gains and losses, and rewards and gifts increased.
translations.idiomatic: He was later summoned to Anfu Hall to debate policy, promoted to gentleman of the masters of writing, where he spoke frankly on what worked and what failed—each time winning richer gifts.

sentences.zh: 常独止宿台上，昼夜不离省闼，帝闻善之。

translations.literal: He often lodged alone on the terrace and day and night did not leave the privy chamber; the emperor heard and praised it.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang often slept alone on the office terrace and never left the inner gate day or night; the emperor heard of it and approved.

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Yongyuan he was appointed left aide.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongyuan 4 he became left aide to the masters of writing.

translations.literal: Merit was full and he ought to have been promoted, but Emperor He retained him and increased his rank.
translations.idiomatic: His tenure merited promotion, yet Emperor He kept him at post and raised his salary instead.

translations.literal: In the sixth year, by cumulative promotion he became overseer of the masters of writing.
translations.idiomatic: In the sixth year he rose step by step to overseer of the masters of writing.

sentences.zh: 后以为东郡太守，香上疏让曰：“臣江淮孤贱，愚□小生，经学行能，无可算录。

translations.literal: Later they intended to make him grand warden of the eastern commandery; Huang Xiang presented a memorial declining, saying: "Your subject is a solitary mean man from the Yangzi and Huai, a foolish young student; in classical learning and conduct and ability there is nothing worth recording,
translations.idiomatic: When the court named Huang Xiang grand warden of Dong commandery, he submitted a memorial begging off: "I am a humble nobody from the southlands, a shallow student; my scholarship and conduct offer nothing worth the archive,

sentences.zh: 遭值太平，先人余福，得以弱冠特蒙征用，连阶累任，遂极台阁。

translations.literal: having met the age of great peace and, through the surplus blessing of former men, been able in the weak-crown years specially to receive summons and employment; step by step I have climbed successive posts, until I have reached the summit of the terrace pavilions.
translations.idiomatic: having lived under an age of peace and ridden my ancestors' lingering fortune; still in my twenties I was singled out for office and climbed every rung until I stood at the head of the secretariat.

sentences.zh: 讫无纤介称，报恩效死，诚不意悟。

translations.literal: To the end there has been no hair's-breadth praise; though I would repay grace with death, sincerely I did not expect to receive this.
translations.idiomatic: I have never earned the slightest praise; I would gladly give my life for the throne, yet I never dreamed I would be singled out for such favor.

sentences.zh: 卒被非望，显拜近郡，尊位千里。

translations.literal: Suddenly I have received what was beyond hope, have been plainly appointed to a nearby commandery, a noble position over a thousand li.
translations.idiomatic: Now I am given what exceeds all hope—a manifest appointment to a neighboring commandery, a thousand-li magistracy.

sentences.zh: 臣闻量能授官，则职无废事；

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that when one matches capacity and confers office, then in duties there are no neglected tasks;
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that offices fit to talent leave no duty undone;

translations.literal: when according to labor one bestows ranks, then worthy and foolish obtain what is fitting.
translations.idiomatic: and that rewards scaled to labor give each man, wise or dull, what he deserves.

sentences.zh: 臣香小丑，少为诸生，典郡从政，固非所堪。

translations.literal: Your subject Huang Xiang is a petty clown; in youth I was a student; to model a commandery and handle government is indeed not what I can bear.
translations.idiomatic: I am a trifling figure who began as a mere student; to govern a whole commandery is more than I can shoulder.

translations.literal: Truly I fear stumbling in office and alone disgracing the sage grace.
translations.idiomatic: I dread I would falter in duty and shame your grace alone.

sentences.zh: 又惟机密端首，至为尊要，复非臣香所当久奉。

translations.literal: Moreover I reflect that the pivot of secret business is supremely venerable and critical, and again it is not what I, Huang Xiang, ought long to hold.
translations.idiomatic: Moreover the pivot of state secrets is the weightiest trust of all—not a burden I should carry long.

translations.literal: Receiving the edict I was alarmed and did not know what to decide.
translations.idiomatic: The edict struck me with panic; I do not know how to answer.

sentences.zh: 臣香年在方刚，适可驱使。

translations.literal: Your subject Huang Xiang's years are in the prime of vigor; just right to be driven and employed.
translations.idiomatic: I am still in the prime of life—fit to run errands for the court, not to rule a commandery.

sentences.zh: 愿乞余恩，留备冗官，赐以督责小职，任之宫台烦事，以毕臣香蝼蚁小志，诚瞑目至愿，土灰极荣。

translations.literal: I beg the remainder of grace, to be kept as a supernumerary official, granted a petty post of supervision and blame, assigned the vexing affairs of the palace terrace, in order to exhaust your subject Huang Xiang's ant-like small ambition—sincerely this is the utmost wish to close my eyes, earth and ash extreme glory.
translations.idiomatic: I beg you leave me a supernumerary slot, some petty supervisory chore, the thankless paper work of the terrace—enough to satisfy my ant's ambition; to die with that would be glory enough for dust and ashes.

sentences.zh: ”帝亦惜香干用，久习旧事，复留为尚书令，增秩二千石，赐钱三十万。

translations.literal: " The emperor also prized Huang Xiang's practical ability, long accustomed to old affairs, again retained him as overseer of the masters of writing, increased his rank to two thousand piculs, and granted three hundred thousand cash.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor valued Huang Xiang's executive skill and long experience with routine, kept him as overseer of the masters of writing, raised his salary to two thousand piculs, and gave him three hundred thousand cash.

sentences.zh: 是后遂管枢机，甚见亲重，而香亦□勤物务，忧公如家。

translations.literal: From this he then managed the pivot mechanism, was greatly seen as intimate and weighty, and Huang Xiang also was diligent in affairs, worrying for the public as for a family.
translations.idiomatic: From then on Huang Xiang turned the central gears of government, won deep trust, and threw himself into every file as if the realm were his own household.

sentences.zh: 十二年，东平清河奏訞言卿仲辽等，所连及且千人。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year, Dongping and Qinghe reported slanderous words implicating Qing Zhongliao and others; those connected reached nearly a thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth year Dongping and Qinghe denounced seditious talk that ensnared Qing Zhongliao and others until nearly a thousand names were caught in the net.

translations.literal: Huang Xiang separately drafted a memorial according to which very many were wholly spared.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang drafted a separate finding that spared a great host of them.

sentences.zh: 每郡国疑罪，辄务求轻科，爱惜人命，每存忧济。

translations.literal: Whenever commanderies and kingdoms had doubtful crimes, he always strove to seek light statutes, cherished human life, and always harbored pity and relief.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever a province sent up an ambiguous case, he always looked for the mildest statute, cherished every life, and leaned toward mercy.

sentences.zh: 又晓习边事，均量军政，皆得事宜。

translations.literal: Again he was thoroughly familiar with border affairs, evenly weighed military government, and all obtained what was fitting.
translations.idiomatic: He knew frontier business inside out and balanced civil and military policy so that each decision fit the facts.

translations.literal: The emperor knew his meticulous diligence and repeatedly added favor and rewards.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor saw his tireless care and heaped favor on him again and again.

translations.literal: When ill he sent inquiries, granted medicines.
translations.idiomatic: When he fell ill the court sent physicians and drugs.

sentences.zh: 在位多所荐达，宠遇甚盛，议者讥其过幸。

translations.literal: In office he many times recommended and advanced men; favor and treatment were very great; discussers ridiculed his excessive good fortune.
translations.idiomatic: In office he lifted many men to promotion; some critics mocked his run of exceptional luck.

translations.literal: In the first year of Yanping he was transferred grand warden of Wei commandery.
translations.idiomatic: In Yanping 1 he became grand warden of Wei commandery.

sentences.zh: 郡旧有内外园田，常与人分种，收谷岁数千斛。

translations.literal: The commandery formerly had inner and outer park fields, constantly shared planting with others, harvesting grain several thousand hu yearly.
translations.idiomatic: The commandery had long kept inner and outer park lands share-cropped with commoners, yielding several thousand hu a year.

sentences.zh: 香曰：“《田令》‘商者不农’，《王制》‘仕者不耕’，伐冰食禄之人，不与百姓争利。

translations.literal: Xiang said: "The Field Ordinance states 'Merchants do not farm'; the Royal Regulations state 'Office-holders do not plough'; men who cut ice and eat stipends ought not contend with the hundred surnames for profit.
translations.idiomatic: Huang Xiang said: "The Field Ordinance says merchants do not till; the Royal Regulations say officials do not plough; men who live on ice-house salaries should not squeeze the commoners for profit."

translations.literal: " Thereupon he entirely assigned them to the people and assessed them to till and plant.
translations.idiomatic: He therefore turned every plot over to the people and taxed only the harvest.

sentences.zh: 时被水年肌，乃分奉禄及所得赏赐班赡贫者，于是丰富之家各出义谷，助官禀贷，荒民获全。

translations.literal: At the time it was a year struck by flood and famine; then he divided his salary and what he had received in gifts and distributed relief to the poor; thereupon rich and ample households each brought forth righteous grain, helped the official granaries lend, and the starving people obtained preservation.
translations.idiomatic: A flood year brought famine; he split his salary and gifts to feed the destitute, and the wealthy families followed suit with "charity grain," refilling the public granaries on loan until the starving were saved.

sentences.zh: 后坐水潦事免，数月，卒于家。

translations.literal: Later because of the flooding affair he was dismissed; within several months he died at home.
translations.idiomatic: He later lost office over the flood case; a few months later he died at home.

sentences.zh: 所著贼、笺、奏、书、令、凡五篇。

translations.literal: What he authored—fu, notes, memorials, letters, commands—totals five pieces.
translations.idiomatic: His extant writings—rhapsodies, notes, memorials, letters, and orders—number five pieces.

translations.literal: His son Qiong has his own biography.
translations.idiomatic: His son Huang Qiong has a separate biography.

translations.literal: Liu Yi was a son of Prince Jing of Beihai.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yi was a son of Prince Jing of Beihai.

sentences.zh: 初封平望侯，永元中，坐事夺爵。

translations.literal: At first ennobled marquis of Pingwang; in the Yongyuan era, because of an affair his noble rank was stripped.
translations.idiomatic: First enfeoffed as marquis of Pingwang, he lost the title during the Yongyuan years over an incident.

translations.literal: Yi in youth had a reputation for literary disputation.
translations.idiomatic: As a youth he was known for eloquence and belles-lettres.

sentences.zh: 元初元年，上《汉德论》并《宪论》十二篇。

translations.literal: In the first year of Yuanchu he presented the "Discourse on Han Virtue" together with twelve pieces of "Discourse on the Model."
translations.idiomatic: In Yuanchu 1 he presented his "Discourse on Han Virtue" and twelve chapters of "Discourse on the Exemplar."

sentences.zh: 时，刘珍、邓耽、尹兑、马融共上书称其美，安帝嘉之，赐钱三万，拜议郎。

translations.literal: At the time Liu Zhen, Deng Dan, Yin Dui, and Ma Rong jointly submitted a memorial praising his excellence; Emperor An commended him, granted thirty thousand cash, and appointed him counsel gentleman.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Zhen, Deng Dan, Yin Dui, and Ma Rong then jointly memorialized his merits; Emperor An approved, gave him thirty thousand cash, and named him counsel gentleman.

sentences.zh: 李尤字伯仁，广汉雒人也。

translations.literal: Li You, courtesy name Boren, was a man of Luo in Guanghan.
translations.idiomatic: Li You, courtesy name Boren, came from Luo in Guanghan commandery.

translations.literal: In youth he was distinguished by letters.
translations.idiomatic: He won notice young for his prose.

sentences.zh: 和帝时，侍中贾逵荐尤有相如、杨雄之风，召诣东观，受诏作赋，拜兰台令史。

translations.literal: Under Emperor He, Palace Attendant Jia Kui recommended that You had the air of Xiangru and Yang Xiong; he was summoned to the Eastern View, received an edict to compose a fu, and was appointed orchid terrace clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor He, Jia Kui praised him as a match for Sima Xiangru and Yang Xiong; the court called him to the Eastern Pavilion, ordered a rhapsody, and named him orchid terrace clerk.

sentences.zh: 稍迁，安帝时为谏议大夫，受诏与谒者仆射刘珍等俱撰《汉记》。

translations.literal: By gradual promotion, under Emperor An he became grandee remonstrant and consultant, received an edict together with the receptionist director Liu Zhen and others jointly to compile the "Han Records."
translations.idiomatic: He rose by degrees to grandee remonstrant under Emperor An and was charged with Liu Zhen and others to draft the Han Records.

sentences.zh: 后帝废太子为济阴王，尤上书谏争。

translations.literal: Later the emperor deposed the heir apparent and made him prince of Jiyin; You submitted a memorial remonstrating and disputing.
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor demoted the heir to prince of Jiyin, Li You sent up a sharp protest.

translations.literal: When Emperor Shun was established, he was promoted minister of Le'an.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Shun he became minister of Le'an.

translations.literal: At age eighty-three he died.
translations.idiomatic: He died at eighty-three.

sentences.zh: 所著诗、赋、铭、诔、颂、《七叹》、《哀典》，凡二十八篇。

translations.literal: What he authored—poems, fu, inscriptions, dirges, odes, "Seven Sighs," "Canon of Lament"—totals twenty-eight pieces.
translations.idiomatic: His poems, rhapsodies, inscriptions, laments, hymns, "Seven Sighs," and "Canon of Lament" come to twenty-eight titles.

sentences.zh: 尤同郡李胜，亦有文才，为东观郎，著赋、诔、颂、论数十篇。

translations.literal: You's fellow commanderyman Li Sheng also had literary talent; he was an Eastern View gentleman and authored several tens of pieces of fu, dirges, odes, and disquisitions.
translations.idiomatic: His townsman Li Sheng was likewise a writer, served as an Eastern View scholar, and left several dozen rhapsodies, laments, hymns, and essays.

sentences.zh: 苏顺字孝山，京兆霸陵人也。

translations.literal: Su Shun, courtesy name Xiaoshan, was a man of Baling in the capital region of Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Su Shun, courtesy name Xiaoshan, was a native of Baling in the metropolitan area.

translations.literal: Between He and An he was praised for talent and learning.
translations.idiomatic: Between the He and An reigns he was celebrated for scholarship.

translations.literal: He loved the arts of nurturing life, hid away and sought the Way.
translations.idiomatic: He loved longevity arts, withdrew from office, and sought the Dao.

translations.literal: Late he then took office, was appointed gentleman of the interior, and died in office.
translations.idiomatic: Only late in life did he enter service as a gentleman of the interior and die in harness.

sentences.zh: 所著贼、论、诔、哀辞、杂文，凡十六篇。

translations.literal: What he authored—memorials, disquisitions, dirges, elegies, miscellaneous pieces—totals sixteen pieces.
translations.idiomatic: His petitions, essays, laments, dirges, and miscellanea number sixteen pieces.

sentences.zh: 时，三辅多士，扶风曹众伯师亦有才学，著诔、书、论四篇。

translations.literal: At the time in the Three Adjuncts there were many gentlemen; Cao Zhong, courtesy name Boshi, of Fufeng also had talent and learning, and authored four pieces of dirge, letter, and disquisition.
translations.idiomatic: The capital districts teemed with talent: Cao Zhong (Boshi) of Fufeng was another noted scholar who left four laments, letters, and treatises.

sentences.zh: 又有曹朔，不知何许人，作《汉颂》四篇。

translations.literal: There was also Cao Shuo, of unknown origin, who composed four pieces of "Han Odes."
translations.idiomatic: There was also Cao Shuo, of unknown home, who wrote four "Odes to Han."

sentences.zh: 葛龚字元甫，梁国宁陵人也。

translations.literal: Ge Gong, courtesy name Yuanfu, was a man of Ningling in the Liang state.
translations.idiomatic: Ge Gong, courtesy name Yuanfu, came from Ningling in the kingdom of Liang.

translations.literal: Under Emperor He he was known for skill in documentary writing.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor He he was famed for crisp administrative prose.

translations.literal: His nature was generous, fierce, and bold; courage and strength surpassed others.
translations.idiomatic: He was bold and forthright by nature, stronger than ordinary men.

sentences.zh: 安帝永初中，举孝廉，为太官丞，上便宜四事，拜荡阴令。

translations.literal: In the early Yongchu of Emperor An, recommended filial and incorrupt, he became aide in the grand provisioner office, presented four matters of convenience, and was appointed magistrate of Tangyin.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Emperor An's Yongchu years he was summoned as filial and incorrupt, served as aide at the imperial kitchen, offered four policy memos, and became magistrate of Tangyin.

translations.literal: He was summoned to the grand commandant's office but was ill and did not go.
translations.idiomatic: The grand commandant summoned him to staff, but illness kept him away.

translations.literal: The province raised him as flourishing talent; he became magistrate of Linfen.
translations.idiomatic: The province next nominated him as flourishing talent and made him magistrate of Linfen.

translations.literal: Dwelling in the two counties, both had praised performance.
translations.idiomatic: In both posts his administration won praise.

sentences.zh: 著文、贼、碑、诔、书记，凡十二篇。

translations.literal: He authored essays, memorials, stelae, dirges, and letters—twelve pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: His essays, petitions, inscriptions, laments, and letters total twelve pieces.

sentences.zh: 王逸字叔师，南郡宜城人也。

translations.literal: Wang Yi, courtesy name Shushi, was a man of Yicheng in Nan commandery.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yi, courtesy name Shushi, was from Yicheng in Nan commandery.

sentences.zh: 元初中，举上计吏，为校书郎。

translations.literal: In the early Yuanchu he was raised as clerk for the capital accounts and became collator.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Yuanchu he was nominated clerk for the capital accounts and appointed collating secretary.

translations.literal: Under Emperor Shun he was palace attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Shun he served as palace attendant.

translations.literal: He authored "Commentary on the Songs of Chu" which circulated in the world.
translations.idiomatic: His Commentary on the Songs of Chu has circulated ever since.

sentences.zh: 其赋、诔、书、论及杂文，凡二十一篇。

translations.literal: His fu, dirges, letters, disquisitions, and miscellaneous pieces total twenty-one.
translations.idiomatic: His rhapsodies, laments, letters, essays, and miscellanea number twenty-one.
