translations.literal: He also composed one hundred twenty-three pieces of "Han Poems."
translations.idiomatic: He also compiled one hundred twenty-three "Han Poems."

translations.literal: His son Yanshou, courtesy name Wenkao, had outstanding talent.
translations.idiomatic: His son Wang Yanshou, courtesy name Wenkao, possessed rare literary gifts.

translations.literal: In youth he traveled in Lu and composed the "Rhapsody on the Hall of Lingguang."
translations.idiomatic: As a youth he studied in Lu and wrote the Rhapsody on the Hall of Lingguang.

sentences.zh: 后蔡邕亦造此赋，未成，及见延寿所为，甚奇之，遂辍翰而已。

translations.literal: Later Cai Yong also undertook this fu; it was not completed, and when he saw what Yanshou had done, he marveled at it greatly, then laid down his brush and stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Yong later attempted the same piece; when he read Yanshou's version he set down his brush in wonder and never finished his own.

sentences.zh: 曾有异梦，意恶之，乃作《梦赋》以自厉。

translations.literal: Once he had a strange dream; his mind thought it ill; therefore he composed the "Dream Fu" to brace himself.
translations.idiomatic: After an ominous dream he wrote the "Dream Rhapsody" to steel his resolve.

translations.literal: Later he drowned and died; at the time of his years he was over twenty.
translations.idiomatic: He later drowned, still in his twenties.

sentences.zh: 崔琦字子玮，涿郡安平人，济北相瑗之宗也。

translations.literal: Cui Qi, courtesy name Ziwei, was a man of Anping in Zhuo commandery, of the lineage of the minister of Jibei, Cui Yuan.
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi, courtesy name Ziwei, was a clansman of Cui Yuan, minister of Jibei, from Anping in Zhuo commandery.

sentences.zh: 少游学京师，以文章博通称。

translations.literal: In youth he traveled and studied at the capital and was praised for broad mastery through letters.
translations.idiomatic: He studied at Luoyang in his youth and was known as a widely read stylist.

translations.literal: At first raised as "examined incorrupt," he became gentleman.
translations.idiomatic: His first nomination was as examined incorrupt, which won him a gentleman's post.

sentences.zh: 河南尹梁冀闻其才，请与交。

translations.literal: The Intendant of Henan, Liang Ji, heard of his talent and requested to associate with him.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji, intendant of Henan, heard of his gifts and pressed for his friendship.

sentences.zh: 冀行多不轨，琦数引古今成败以戒之，冀不能受。

translations.literal: Ji's conduct was often not in bounds; Qi repeatedly cited ancient and modern success and failure to warn him; Ji could not accept it.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji's behavior skirted treason; Cui Qi again and again cited historical parallels, but Ji would not listen.

translations.literal: Thereupon he composed the "Admonition to the Maternal Kin."
translations.idiomatic: He therefore wrote the Admonition to the Maternal Kin.

translations.literal: Its wording says.
translations.idiomatic: The text runs as follows.

translations.literal: Ho, ho—the maternal kin—splendid favor blazing bright.
translations.idiomatic: Hearken, you who bask in palace favor—your glory blazes too bright.

translations.literal: In antiquity under Emperor Shun, virtue flourished with Ying and Huang.
translations.idiomatic: In Shun's day virtue shone through the Ying and Huang clans.

translations.literal: Zhou rose with three mothers; there was Shen who honored Tang.
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou house rose with three royal mothers; the lady of Shen exalted Tang.

translations.literal: King Xuan rose late; Queen Jiang removed her hairpins.
translations.idiomatic: When King Xuan of Zhou slept in, Queen Jiang of Qi pulled out her pins to shame him awake.

translations.literal: Duke Huan of Qi loved music; the lady of Wei gave no sound.
translations.idiomatic: Duke Huan of Qi doted on music; his Wei consort refused to play for him until he returned to duty.

sentences.zh: 皆辅主以礼，扶君以仁，达才进善，以义济身。

translations.literal: All aided the ruler with ritual, supported the lord with benevolence, advanced talent and brought forward the good, and with rightness sustained their persons.
translations.idiomatic: Each aided her lord with ritual, steadied him with kindness, advanced worthies, and kept herself within the bounds of duty.

translations.literal: Reaching to the failing twig, gradually there was already decline and loss.
translations.idiomatic: But by the withered twig of each line decay had already set in.

translations.literal: The string of fish was not ordered; the nine concubines were out of rank.
translations.idiomatic: The harem lost its proper order; the nine ranks of consorts fell into chaos.

translations.literal: The disaster of the Jin state—calamity arose from Li.
translations.idiomatic: Jin's catastrophe began with Consort Li.

translations.literal: As the Classic says, "only the family's cord."
translations.idiomatic: As the Classic warns, "only the family's cord"—the house unravels.

translations.literal: The hen's morning crow.
translations.idiomatic: The hen that crows at dawn—women seizing the hour.

translations.literal: Monopolizing power and selfish favor, making oneself plain and blocking others.
translations.idiomatic: They monopolized power and private favor, flaunted themselves, and blocked every rival.

translations.literal: Bullying elders and alienating the old, stripping and peeling the closest kin.
translations.idiomatic: They browbeat elders, sowed discord with old allies, and tore their own kin bare.

translations.literal: Pairing co-equal empresses with the heir's rank, a licentious woman brought destruction to the state of Chen.
translations.idiomatic: When two queens rivaled the heir's station and a wanton favorite ruled the harem, the state of Chen fell to ruin.

translations.literal: The unworthy were raised on high; Fan became minister of education.
translations.idiomatic: Mediocrities rose to power; men like Fan Huo climbed to steward the realm.

translations.literal: Bearing noble rank while riding beyond their station, they drew stipends from famous capitals.
translations.idiomatic: They loaded themselves with titles their shoulders could not bear and fed from the richest commanderies.

translations.literal: The poets therefore satirized them; virtue found no safe harbor.
translations.idiomatic: The Odes skewered such houses, for virtue could find no resting place among them.

translations.literal: The cruel last king of Shang was bewitched by a woman, rejected remonstrance, and isolated himself.
translations.idiomatic: King Zhou of Shang drowned in a consort's flattery, spurned every warning, and cut himself off from the world.

translations.literal: Bat and serpent were his heart; he unleashed poison and spared no innocent.
translations.idiomatic: His heart was viper-cold; he poured out cruelty and killed without cause.

translations.literal: He killed his paternal uncles; he carved open women with child.
translations.idiomatic: He butchered his own uncles and ripped the bellies of pregnant women.

translations.literal: Heaven raged and earth resented; men plotted and ghosts schemed against him.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth turned against him; living men and vengeful shades alike conspired for his fall.

translations.literal: On the jiazi day at cockcrow, body and head were parted.
translations.idiomatic: At dawn on the day jiazi his head rolled from his shoulders.

translations.literal: First he had been Son of Heaven; afterward he became a man-dragon thrall.
translations.idiomatic: He had worn the crown of heaven; in the end he was less than a slave—mockery made a monster of a king.

translations.literal: It was not only indulgence in beauty—the empress dowagers were especially so.
translations.idiomatic: The vice was not lust alone; the palace matrons outdid one another in it.

sentences.zh: 不相率以礼，而竞奖以权。

translations.literal: They did not lead one another by ritual but vied for reward through power.
translations.idiomatic: Instead of guiding the court by rite, they fought for favor with naked force.

translations.literal: First they laughed, then they wailed; in the end they ended in shame and mutilation.
translations.idiomatic: They laughed while fortune lasted, then howled when the blade fell—every house ended in disgrace and the butcher's block.

translations.literal: The altars of state were snuffed out; the ancestral temple was put to the torch.
translations.idiomatic: Dynastic fires went out and imperial shrines blazed to ash.

sentences.zh: 末嬉丧夏，褒姒毙周，妲已亡殷，赵灵沙丘。

translations.literal: Moxi destroyed Xia, Baosi destroyed Zhou, Daji destroyed Yin, King Ling of Zhao perished on the sands of Dune.
translations.idiomatic: Moxi sank the Xia, Baosi broke the Zhou, Daji poisoned the Shang, and King Ling of Zhao breathed his last on the dunes of Shaqiu.

translations.literal: Lady Qi was made a human pig; the house of Lu thereby failed.
translations.idiomatic: Consort Qi became Empress Lü's "human swine," and the Lü clan paid for it with extinction.

translations.literal: Empress Chen practiced witchcraft and in the end died outside.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Chen's sorcery drove her from the palace to die in exile.

translations.literal: Huo wished to poison the heir; his own person then suffered ruin.
translations.idiomatic: Huo Chengsi plotted to poison the crown prince—and brought ruin on himself.

sentences.zh: 故曰：无谓我贵，天将尔摧；

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: "Do not say, 'I am noble'—Heaven will crush you;
translations.idiomatic: Hence the warning: "Never boast of your height—Heaven stoops to strike the proud."

translations.literal: "Do not trust lasting beauty—color has its waning and fading."
translations.idiomatic: "Never trust a face that will not fade—beauty always gutters out."

translations.literal: "Do not rely on lasting favor—love has its delay and decline."
translations.idiomatic: "Never lean on a sovereign's whim—royal love slackens like a loosened cord."

translations.literal: "Do not say, 'I am capable'—Heaven and men will turn away from you."
translations.idiomatic: "Never cry 'I alone am wise'—Heaven and the people will abandon you."

translations.literal: Calamity is born of want of virtue; fortune has its careful pivot.
translations.idiomatic: Disaster sprouts where virtue is thin; good fortune hinges on a hair.

translations.literal: The sun does not long stand at the meridian; the moon at the full must wane.
translations.idiomatic: The sun does not pause at noon; the full moon must shrink again.

translations.literal: He who treads the Way stands firm; he who leans on mere power stands in peril.
translations.idiomatic: Walk the Way and you stand on rock; lean on brute force and you tread ice.

translations.literal: Your petty servant oversees the maternal kin and ventures to report thus.
translations.idiomatic: I, a minor officer charged with kin relations, lay this before you.

sentences.zh: 琦以言不从，失意，复作《白鹄赋》以为风。

translations.literal: Qi, because his words were not followed, was disappointed and again composed the "Rhapsody of the White Crane" as a wind-remonstrance.
translations.idiomatic: When Liang Ji ignored him, Cui Qi sulked and wrote the White Crane Rhapsody as a veiled rebuke.

sentences.zh: 梁冀见之，呼琦问曰：“百官外内，各有司存，天下云云，岂独吾人之尤，君何激刺之过乎！

translations.literal: Liang Ji saw it, called Qi in and asked: "Officials within and without each have their office; the world murmurs—could the blame be ours alone? Why such excessive biting satire!
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji read it, summoned Cui Qi, and snapped: "Every bureau has its brief; the empire buzzes with gossip—do you think we alone are at fault? What gives you the right to slash so deep?"

sentences.zh: ”琦对曰：“昔管仲相齐，乐闻机谏之言；

translations.literal: Qi replied: "In olden days Guan Zhong assisted Qi and was glad to hear covert remonstrance;
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi answered: "When Guan Zhong served Duke Huan he welcomed even whispered correction;

sentences.zh: 萧何佐汉，乃设书过之吏。

translations.literal: Xiao He assisted Han and therefore set up clerks to record faults.
translations.idiomatic: Xiao He aided the Han founder and posted clerks whose sole duty was to note his missteps.

sentences.zh: 今将军累世台辅，任齐伊、公，而德政未闻，黎元涂炭。

translations.literal: Now the general for generations has been pillar at the terrace; his burden matches Yi Yin and the Duke, yet no virtuous government is heard and the black-haired people are in mud and charcoal.
translations.idiomatic: Your house has propped the throne for generations; your charge rivals Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou—yet the people hear no mercy from your rule, only fire and mire.

sentences.zh: 不能结纳贞良，以救祸败，反复欲钳塞士口，杜蔽主听，将使玄黄改色，马鹿易形乎？

translations.literal: You cannot gather in the chaste and good to save calamity and ruin; instead you would pinch shut gentlemen's mouths, block the ruler's hearing—do you mean to turn heaven and earth on their heads and make deer pass for horses?
translations.idiomatic: You will not bind honest men to you to stave off ruin; you would rather gag every scholar and deafen the throne—until black becomes yellow and a stag is sold as a horse?

translations.literal: Ji had nothing to answer and therefore sent Qi home.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji had no reply and dismissed him.

sentences.zh: 后除为临济长，不敢之职，解印绶去。

translations.literal: Later he was appointed magistrate of Linji but dared not take office, surrendered the seal-cord and departed.
translations.idiomatic: He was later named magistrate of Linji but refused the post, laid down his seal, and walked away.

translations.literal: Ji thereupon ordered assassins secretly to seek and kill him.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Ji then sent killers to hunt him down.

sentences.zh: 客见琦耕于陌上，怀书一卷，息辄偃而咏之。

translations.literal: The assassin saw Qi plowing on a field path, a bundle of books at his breast; when he rested he lay back and chanted them.
translations.idiomatic: One assassin found him furrowing a lane with a satchel of texts; at each pause he lay in the dust and recited aloud.

sentences.zh: 客哀其志，以实告琦，曰：“将军令吾要子，今见君贤者，情怀忍忍。

translations.literal: The guest pitied his purpose and truthfully told Qi, saying: "The general ordered me to cut you off; now seeing you a worthy man, my heart cannot bear it.
translations.idiomatic: The man pitied such single-mindedness and confessed: "The general sent me to kill you; seeing a scholar of your stamp, I cannot strike.

sentences.zh: 可亟自逃，吾亦于此亡矣。

translations.literal: Hurry and flee; I too will die here.
translations.idiomatic: Run now—I shall die here in your place.

translations.literal: Qi obtained escape and fled; afterward Ji still caught and killed him.
translations.idiomatic: Cui Qi escaped, but Liang Ji's agents caught him in the end and put him to death.

sentences.zh: 所著赋、颂、铭、诔、箴、吊、论、《九咨》、《七言》，凡十五篇。

translations.literal: What he authored—fu, odes, inscriptions, dirges, admonitions, condolences, disquisitions, "Nine Consultations," "Seven Lines"—totals fifteen pieces.
translations.idiomatic: His rhapsodies, hymns, inscriptions, laments, admonitions, elegies, essays, Nine Consultations, and Seven Lines number fifteen titles.

sentences.zh: 边韶字孝先，陈留浚仪人也。

translations.literal: Bian Shao, courtesy name Xiaoxian, was a man of Junyi in Chenliu.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao, courtesy name Xiaoxian, came from Junyi in Chenliu commandery.

sentences.zh: 以文章知名，教授数百人。

translations.literal: He was known for letters and taught several hundred men.
translations.idiomatic: He won fame as a writer and kept several hundred pupils.

sentences.zh: 韶口辩，曾昼日假卧，弟子私嘲之曰：“边孝先，腹便便。

translations.literal: Shao was eloquent in debate; once he feigned sleep by day; disciples privately mocked him, saying: "Bian Xiaoxian—belly so round.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao was quick of tongue; one noon he pretended to nap, and his students whispered, "Bian Xiaoxian—what a round belly.

translations.literal: Lazy to read books—only wants to sleep.
translations.idiomatic: Too lazy to read—only good for snoring.

sentences.zh: ”韶潜闻之，应时对曰：“边为姓、考为字。

translations.literal: Shao overheard and answered on the spot: "Bian is the surname; Xian is the courtesy name.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao heard them and shot back: "Bian is my clan, Xian my style.

translations.literal: Belly so round—the chest for the Five Classics.
translations.idiomatic: This belly is the coffer of the Five Classics.

translations.literal: Only wanting to sleep—pondering the classics.
translations.idiomatic: This nap is meditation on the canon.

sentences.zh: 寐与周公通梦，静与孔子同意。

translations.literal: In dreams I converse with the Duke of Zhou; in stillness I share intentions with Confucius.
translations.idiomatic: Asleep I trade words with the Duke of Zhou; awake my mind walks with Confucius.

translations.literal: If the teacher may be mocked—from what canon does that come?
translations.idiomatic: Tell me which classic licenses students to mock their master?

translations.literal: The mockers were greatly ashamed.
translations.idiomatic: The students crept away in shame.

translations.literal: Shao's quick talent was all of this kind.
translations.idiomatic: Bian Shao's wit was always that sharp.

sentences.zh: 桓帝时，为临颍侯相，征拜太中大夫，著作东观。

translations.literal: Under Emperor Huan he was minister to the Marquis of Linying, was summoned as grandee of the palace, and composed at the Eastern View.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Huan he served the Marquis of Linying as minister, was called to court as grandee of the palace, and wrote at the Eastern Pavilion.

sentences.zh: 再迁北地太守，入拜尚书令。

translations.literal: Twice promoted he became grand warden of Beidi; he entered and was appointed overseer of the masters of writing.
translations.idiomatic: He rose twice to grand warden of Beidi, then entered the capital as overseer of the masters of writing.

translations.literal: Later he was minister of Chen and died in office.
translations.idiomatic: He ended as minister of Chen and died in harness.

sentences.zh: 著诗、颂、碑、铭、书、策，凡十五篇。

translations.literal: He authored poems, odes, stelae, inscriptions, letters, and policy memorials—fifteen pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: His poems, hymns, inscriptions, laments, letters, and memorials fill fifteen pieces.
